label: lem:even-necessary
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:even-necessary}
If $w$ is a~shuffle square, then $|w|_{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}}$ is even for~every letter~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}$. In~particular, every shuffle square has even length.

label: ex:1221
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:1221}
The~word $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1221}}$ contains two copies of~each letter but is not a~shuffle square.  A~root would have one~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1}}$ and one~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{2}}$, so it would be either $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{12}}$ or $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{21}}$.  The~last~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1}}$ cannot belong to~a~copy of~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{12}}$, and the~first~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1}}$ cannot belong to~a~copy of~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{21}}$.
head: environment

label: lem:closure-shuffle
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:closure-shuffle}
Let $u$ and $v$ be shuffle squares.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item Their concatenation $uv$ is a~shuffle square.
\item Their reversals $\operatorname{rev}(u)$ and $\operatorname{rev}(v)$ are shuffle squares.
\item Their binary complements $\overline u$ and $\overline v$ are shuffle squares.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: If $u$ is a~self-shuffle of~$x$ and $v$ is a~self-shuffle of~$y$, then the~two chosen copies in~$u$ followed by~the~corresponding two copies in~$v$ show that $uv$ is a~self-shuffle of~$xy$. Reversing a~coloring that decomposes $u$ into two copies of~$x$ gives a~coloring that decomposes $\operatorname{rev}(u)$ into two copies of~$\operatorname{rev}(x)$. Applying the~same letter permutation to~both copies gives a~coloring of~$\overline u$ by~two copies of~$\overline x$, and similarly for~$v$.
head: environment

label: prop:residual-test
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:residual-test}
A~nonempty word $w$ is a~shuffle square if and only if $\varepsilon\in\mathcal{Q}_{|w|}(w)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that a~coloring of~the~first~$i$ positions has produced two prefix-comparable subwords.  Removing their common prefix leaves a~unique residual word~$q$, together with~the~information of~which color is longer. Appending $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{w}}_{i+1}$ to~the~longer color gives the~first transition in~\eqref{eq:residual-recurrence2}.  Appending it to~the~shorter color is possible precisely if it cancels the~first letter of~$q$, giving the~second transition.  Thus every path in~the~recurrence records an~actual partial coloring, and every prefix-comparable partial coloring gives such a~path.

In~any successful coloring, both partial subwords after~$i$ positions are prefixes of~the~same final root.  Hence they are necessarily prefix-comparable.  At~the~end they are equal exactly when the~residual word is empty.  This proves both implications.
head: environment

label: rem:residual-pruning
title: Remark
head: environment

label: prop:run-recognizer
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:run-recognizer}
The~procedure in~Listing~\ref{lst:run-test} returns true exactly for~the~nonempty shuffle squares.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Every shuffle square admits a~canonical pair of~perfect twins with~$i_\ell<j_\ell$ for~every~$\ell$. Indeed, pair the~positions carrying corresponding letters of~the~two equal copies and replace each pair by~its left and right endpoint. Since the~two original support sequences are increasing, the~sequences of~left and right endpoints are also increasing, and both still induce the~same word. If within one run a~second-copy position precedes a~first-copy position, interchange their assignments. The~letters are equal, so neither induced word changes. Moreover, the~first-copy count at every initial cut can only increase. Repeating removes all such inversions.

Now scan the~canonical pair just constructed from~left to~right. The~partial second copy is always a~prefix of~the~partial first copy. Let~$q$ be the~unmatched suffix. A~run $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}^r$ is split into $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}^x$ assigned to~the~first copy followed by~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}^y$ assigned to~the~second, where $x+y=r$. After the~first assignment the~unmatched word is $q\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}^x$. The~second assignment is possible exactly when $q\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}^x$ begins with~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}^y$, and deleting this prefix gives the~new residual. This is precisely one transition of~Listing~\ref{lst:run-test}. A~residual longer than the~unprocessed part cannot be cancelled and is discarded without loss, exactly as~in~Remark~\ref{rem:residual-pruning}. Thus canonical perfect twins give a~path from~$\varepsilon$ to~$\varepsilon$. Conversely, every such path specifies the~splits of~all runs and maintains the~prefix invariant, hence constructs two equal subwords partitioning all positions.
head: environment

label: ex:length8
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:length8}
For~$w=P_8=\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{12211212}}$, recurrence \eqref{eq:residual-recurrence2} gives
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{Q}_0&=\{\varepsilon\},\quad
\mathcal{Q}_1=\{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1}}\},\quad
\mathcal{Q}_2=\{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{12}}\},\quad
\mathcal{Q}_3=\{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{122}}\},\quad
\mathcal{Q}_4=\{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{22}},\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1221}}\},\\
\mathcal{Q}_5&=\{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{221}},\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{12211}}\},\quad
\mathcal{Q}_6=\{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{21}},\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{2212}},\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{122112}}\},\quad
\mathcal{Q}_7=\{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{211}},\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{22112}},\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{22121}},\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1221121}}\},\\
\mathcal{Q}_8&=\{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{11}},\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{2112}},\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{2121}},\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{221122}},\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{221212}},\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{12211212}}\}.
\end{align*}
Since $\varepsilon\notin\mathcal{Q}_8$, the~word $P_8$ is not a~shuffle square. The~same computation at~length~$4$ gives $\mathcal{Q}_4(\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1221}})=\{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{22}},\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1221}}\}$, in~agreement with~Example~\ref{ex:1221}.

For~comparison, the~positive example $v=\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1212}}$ gives
\begin{align*}
  \mathcal{Q}_0(v)=\{\varepsilon\},\quad
  \mathcal{Q}_1(v)=\{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1}}\},\quad
  \mathcal{Q}_2(v)=\{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{12}}\},\quad
  \mathcal{Q}_3(v)=\{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{2}},\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{121}}\},\quad 
  \mathcal{Q}_4(v)=\{\varepsilon,\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{22}},\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1212}}\}.
\end{align*}
Here $\varepsilon\in\mathcal{Q}_4(v)$.  Indeed, the~supports $\{1,2\}$ and $\{3,4\}$ both induce the~root~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{12}}$.

label: def:derivative
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:derivative}
The~finite derivative $D(w)$ of~a~binary word~$w$ is defined as~follows. If one of~the~runs of~$w$ has length greater than~$2$, then $D(w)$ is undefined.  Otherwise start with~$\Delta(w)$, delete its first symbol if that symbol is~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1}}$, and then delete its last symbol if that symbol is~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1}}$. A~single symbol is deleted at~most once.  We also put $D(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon$.

label: prop:even-gap
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Group the~letters of~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\boldsymbol{\mathsf{K}}}$ into~aligned pairs
\begin{align*}
  B_j=\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\boldsymbol{\mathsf{K}}}_{2j-1}\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\boldsymbol{\mathsf{K}}}_{2j}\qquad(j\geqslant1).
\end{align*}
When one passes from~$P_{2j-2}$ to~$P_{2j}$, the~parity of~the~number of~ones changes exactly when $B_j$ is mixed, that is, when $B_j\in\{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{12}},\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{21}}\}$.  An~equal pair $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{11}}$ or $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{22}}$ leaves this parity unchanged.

Start at~an~element $e\in\operatorname{EPK}$.  If the~next aligned pair is equal, then $e+2\in\operatorname{EPK}$.  Otherwise the~next pair is mixed and the~parity becomes odd. There cannot be three consecutive equal aligned pairs.  Indeed, equal aligned pairs are full runs, since all runs of~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\boldsymbol{\mathsf{K}}}$ have length at~most~$2$. Consecutive equal pairs must alternate between $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{11}}$ and~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{22}}$.  Three consecutive equal pairs would therefore give three consecutive runs of~length~$2$.  Their run lengths would produce the~factor $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{222}}$ in~$\Delta(\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\boldsymbol{\mathsf{K}}})=\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\boldsymbol{\mathsf{K}}}$, impossible because every run of~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\boldsymbol{\mathsf{K}}}$ has length at~most~$2$.

Consequently, after a~mixed pair, another mixed pair must occur within the~next three aligned pairs.  At~that second mixed pair the~parity returns to~even.

Thus parity returns after at~most four aligned pairs, proving $e'-e\leqslant8$.  Since $4\in\operatorname{EPK}$, the~argument can be iterated indefinitely.

label: cor:stable-regime
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:stable-regime}
For~every $k\geqslant3$, an~even-Parikh $\mathcal{C}^k$-word of~length greater than~$16$ is a~shuffle square. The~threshold~$16$ and the~set of exactly~$34$ nonempty exceptions are the~same for~all $k\geqslant3$ and for~smooth words.
head: environment

label: cor:factorwise-parity
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:factorwise-parity}
Let $X$ be either a~finite $\mathcal{C}^k$-word for~some $k\geqslant3$, or a right-infinite smooth binary word. Every factor~$u$ of~$X$ with $|u|>16$ is a~shuffle square if and only if its Parikh vector is even.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: In~the~finite case, Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-closure}(i) makes~$u$ a $\mathcal{C}^k$-word and hence a~$C^3$-word. In~the~right-infinite case, Proposition~\ref{prop:infinite-factors-smooth} makes~$u$ smooth. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:C3-parity} and Lemma~\ref{lem:even-necessary}.

\label{lem:C2-local}
Every $C^2$-word of~length~$40$ has a~nonempty shuffle-square prefix and a~nonempty shuffle-square suffix. The~constant~$40$ is optimal.
head: environment

label: eq:C2-bad39
title: Proof

label: cor:C2-factorization
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Repeatedly remove the~shortest nonempty shuffle-square prefix. Every intermediate remainder and every removed block is a~$C^2$ factor by Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-closure}(i). Lemma~\ref{lem:C2-local} bounds each chosen block by~$40$ and the~terminal remainder by~$39$. Concatenation gives the~last assertion about $S_1\cdots S_k$. The~word in
\eqref{eq:C2-bad39} proves sharpness of~the~remainder bound.
Table~\ref{tab:minimal-suffixes} contains eight minimal suffix squares of~length~$40$. Their reversals are minimal shuffle-square prefixes, proving sharpness of~the~block bound.
head: environment

label: lem:C2-reduction
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:C2-reduction}
Let $w\in\mathcal{C}^2$ have even Parikh vector, suppose that $w$ is not a shuffle square, and assume $|w|\geqslant40$. Then $w=us$ for~some $s\in\mathcal M$, where $u\in\mathcal{C}^2$ also has even Parikh vector and is not a~shuffle square.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By~Lemma~\ref{lem:C2-local}, the~length-$40$ suffix factor of~$w$ has a nonempty shuffle-square suffix. Choose a~shortest nonempty shuffle-square suffix~$s$ of~$w$. Then $|s|\leqslant40$ and $s\in\mathcal M$. Write $w=us$. Since $w$ is not a~shuffle square, $s\ne w$, so~$u$ is nonempty. Factoriality gives $u\in\mathcal{C}^2$. Both $w$ and~$s$ have even Parikh vector, hence so does~$u$. If $u$ were a~shuffle square, then $w=us$ would be one by~Lemma~\ref{lem:closure-shuffle}(i), a contradiction.
head: environment

label: thm:C2-parity
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:C2-parity}
Let $w\in\mathcal{C}^2$ and $|w|>48$. Then $w$ is a~shuffle square if and only if its Parikh vector is even. The~bound~$48$ is sharp. Moreover, there are exactly~$212$ nonempty even-Parikh $C^2$-words which are not shuffle squares.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Only sufficiency requires proof. Listing~\ref{lst:parity-levels} gives all~$208$ exceptions of~length below~$40$. Lemma~\ref{lem:C2-reduction} shows that every longer exception can be reduced, by~deleting a~member of~$\mathcal M$, to~a~shorter exception. Repeating eventually reaches~$E_0$, so every exception of~length at least~$40$ belongs to~one of~the~layers in~\eqref{eq:C2-layers}. Listing~\ref{lst:C2-extension} gives $|E_1|=4$ and $E_2=\varnothing$, so there is no further layer. Thus the~complete exceptional set is $E_0\cup E_1$, of~cardinality $208+4=212$. Its longest members are $X_{48}$ and~$\overline X_{48}$, proving both the criterion above length~$48$ and sharpness.

The~finite verification consists of the~proved reduction, the~complete construction in~Listing~\ref{lst:C2-extension}, and the~five exact cardinalities displayed above. No unbounded search is being inferred from a~cutoff.
head: environment

label: thm:C1-reduction
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:C1-reduction}
Let $w\in\mathcal{C}^1$ have even Parikh vector and suppose that it is not a shuffle square. If $|w|\geqslant36$, then $w$ has a~proper nonempty shuffle-square prefix and a~proper nonempty shuffle-square suffix. The maximum length of~an~even-Parikh $C^1$-word with no such prefix is~$34$, so~$36$ is the~sharp threshold among admissible (even) lengths. Moreover, there are exactly~$230$ nonempty even-Parikh $C^1$-words having no nonempty shuffle-square prefix, and all of~them have length at~most~$34$.
head: environment

label: eq:C1-bad-counts
title: Proof

label: cor:C1-factorization
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Repeatedly remove the~shortest nonempty shuffle-square prefix. Every remainder is a~$C^1$ factor and retains an~even Parikh vector. At termination, a~nonempty remainder has no nonempty shuffle-square prefix and is therefore one of the~$230$ words in Table~\ref{tab:C1-even-bad}. Concatenation of~the~$S_i$ proves that $r=\varepsilon$ would make~$w$ a~shuffle square.

For~the~absence of~a block bound, put
\begin{align*}
 U=\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{12}}(\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1122}})^9,
 \qquad Y_m=U(\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1122}})^m\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{12}}\quad(m\geqslant0).
\end{align*}
The~word~$U$ is one of~the first-class seeds above and reaches residual~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{12}}$. The~pumping and exit identities in \eqref{eq:C1-pump-one} show that every~$Y_m$ is a~$C^1$ shuffle square, whereas every proper nonempty prefix lies on the~bad ray from~$U$. Thus $Y_m$ is a~minimal shuffle-square prefix of~length~$40+4m$.

label: prop:boundary-local
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:boundary-local}
Let $w=\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{w}}_1\cdots \textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{w}}_n$ be a~finite $C^3$-word.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item For~every $1\leqslant i\leqslant n-23$, some factor beginning at~position~$i$ is a~shuffle square of~length in~$\{2,4,\ldots,24\}$.
\item For~every $24\leqslant j\leqslant n$, some factor ending at~position~$j$ is a~shuffle square of~length in~$\{2,4,\ldots,24\}$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, a~$C^3$-word of~length~$n\geqslant24$ contains at~least $n-23$ shuffle-square occurrences with~distinct starting positions.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: For~(i), the~length-$24$ factor $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{w}}_i\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{w}}_{i+1}\cdots \textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{w}}_{i+23}$ belongs to~$\mathcal{C}^3$ by~Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-closure}(i). Apply the~prefix part of~Lemma~\ref{lem:C3-local}. Part~(ii) follows from~the~suffix part applied to~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{w}}_{j-23}\cdots \textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{w}}_j$. The~final count chooses one occurrence for~each of~the~$n-23$ possible starting positions in~(i). Occurrences with~different starting positions are different intervals.
head: environment

label: thm:finite-factorization
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Start with~the~remainder $r_0=w$. If $r_{i-1}$ has a~nonempty shuffle-square prefix, let $S_i$ be its shortest such prefix and write $r_{i-1}=S_ir_i$. The~choices are deterministic, and the~length strictly decreases, so the~process terminates in~a~remainder~$r$ with~no such prefix. Every intermediate remainder and every selected block is a~factor of~$w$, hence belongs to~$\mathcal{C}^3$ by~Lemma~\ref{lem:smooth-closure}(i). The~same lemma preserves any stronger class~$\mathcal{C}^k$ and smoothness.

If an~intermediate remainder has length at~least~$24$, its first~$24$ letters form a~$C^3$-word and Lemma~\ref{lem:C3-local} supplies a~shuffle-square prefix of~length at~most~$24$. Thus every chosen shortest block has length at~most~$24$, and a~terminal remainder cannot have length at~least~$24$. The~lower bound~$2$ follows from~Lemma~\ref{lem:even-necessary}. Repeated use of~Lemma~\ref{lem:closure-shuffle}(i) proves~(iii).

When $n\geqslant24$, at~least one block is removed and $|S_1\cdots S_k|=n-|r|\geqslant n-23$. Applying the~established prefix statement to~$\operatorname{rev}(w)$, then using Lemmas~\ref{lem:smooth-closure}(ii) and~\ref{lem:closure-shuffle}(ii), gives the~suffix statement.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The~constant~$23$ in~Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-factorization} is optimal even for~smooth words. Each word in~\eqref{eq:bad23} is smooth and has no nonempty shuffle-square prefix, so its greedy factorization has no block and leaves the~entire length-$23$ word as~its remainder.

label: def:24-local
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:24-local}
A~right-infinite or bi-infinite binary word~$X$ is \emph{length-$24$ locally~$C^3$} if every factor of~$X$ of~length~$24$ belongs to~$\mathcal{C}^3$. Any word whose length-$24$ factors belong to~$\mathcal{C}^k$ for~some $k\geqslant3$ has this property. Proposition~\ref{prop:infinite-factors-smooth} shows the~same for~every smooth right-infinite word.
head: environment

label: thm:infinite-factorization
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Once $s_{k-1}$ is defined, the~length-$24$ factor beginning at~$s_{k-1}+1$ belongs to~$\mathcal{C}^3$. Lemma~\ref{lem:C3-local} gives a~nonempty shuffle-square prefix, so the~least~$d_k$ exists and is at~most~$24$. It is at~least~$2$ by~parity. The~cumulative factor is the~concatenation of~the~first $k$ shuffle-square blocks, hence is a~shuffle square by~Lemma~\ref{lem:closure-shuffle}(i).

Writing $L_k=s_k-t+1=d_1+\cdots+d_k$, we have $L_k\leqslant24k$. For~$k=\lfloor N/24\rfloor$, the~$k$ distinct lengths $L_1,\ldots,L_k$ are all at~most~$N$ (with~the~assertion empty when $k=0$). This proves the~lower bound in~\eqref{eq:local-density}.  Its upper bound follows from~Lemma~\ref{lem:even-necessary}, since only even lengths can be shuffle-square lengths.  Dividing by~$N$ and taking lower and upper limits gives the~final chain of~inequalities.
head: environment

label: cor:bi-infinite
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Starting at~$c_0$, construct the~cuts to~the~right by~the~proof of~Theorem~\ref{thm:infinite-factorization}. Given a~cut on~the~leftward side, apply the~suffix part of~Lemma~\ref{lem:C3-local} to~the~length-$24$ factor ending at~that cut and move left by~the~length of~a~shortest shuffle-square suffix. This constructs all negative-indexed cuts, with~the~same bounds.

label: cor:C2-infinite-factorization
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:C2-infinite-factorization}
Call a~right-infinite or bi-infinite word \emph{length-$40$ locally~$C^2$} when each of~its length-$40$ factors belongs to~$\mathcal{C}^2$. Then all conclusions of~Theorem~\ref{thm:infinite-factorization} and Corollary~\ref{cor:bi-infinite} remain valid after replacing ``length-$24$ locally~$C^3$'' by~``length-$40$ locally~$C^2$'', the~upper block bound~$24$ by~$40$, and the~lower density bound~$1/24$ by~$1/40$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The~proofs are unchanged, with Lemma~\ref{lem:C2-local} supplying a~shuffle-square prefix or suffix of~length at~most~$40$ at~each step.

title: Proof
body_md:
If $P_m$ is a~shuffle square, then $m\in\operatorname{EPK}$ by~Lemma~\ref{lem:even-necessary}.  The~two exceptional values are established in~Examples~\ref{ex:1221} and~\ref{ex:length8}.

Conversely, let $m\in\operatorname{EPK}\setminus\{4,8\}$. Equation~\eqref{eq:small-EPK} shows that either $m=16$ or $m\geqslant20$. The~case $m=16$ is Example~\ref{ex:first-decomposition}. In~the~remaining cases, $P_m$ is a~smooth factor of~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\boldsymbol{\mathsf{K}}}$ by~Corollary~\ref{cor:K-factors-smooth}, hence belongs to~$\mathcal{C}^3$. It has length greater than~$16$ and even Parikh vector. It is therefore a~shuffle square by~Theorem~\ref{thm:C3-parity}.

label: cor:kolakoski-density
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The~displayed sequence follows from~Theorem~\ref{thm:main-intro}, and~\eqref{eq:EPKterms}. Infinitude and the~gap bound follow from~Proposition~\ref{prop:even-gap}. If the~displayed lengths are $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}_1<\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}_2<\cdots$, then $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}_1=16$ and $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}_j\leqslant16+8(j-1)$.  Taking $j=1+\lfloor(N-16)/8\rfloor$ proves~\eqref{eq:K-density}.  The~lower-density bound follows after division by~$N$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Corollary~\ref{cor:K-factors-smooth} makes~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\boldsymbol{\mathsf{K}}}$ length-$24$ locally~$C^3$. Theorem~\ref{thm:infinite-factorization}, with~$X=\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\boldsymbol{\mathsf{K}}}$ and $t=1$, proves that the~recursion is defined, gives the~block-length bounds, and makes every cumulative prefix a~shuffle square. Hence $s_k\in\operatorname{EPK}\setminus\{4,8\}$ for~every $k\geqslant1$ by~Theorem~\ref{thm:main-intro}.

The~initial values above are obtained by~successively applying the~exact recognizer in~Listing~\ref{lst:residual-test} to~the~even-length candidate blocks.

Finally, $s_1=16$ and $P_{20}=P_{16}\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1221}}$. The~word $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1221}}$ has no nonempty shuffle-square prefix by~Example~\ref{ex:1221}, so~$20$ is not a~recursive endpoint, although $P_{20}$ is a~shuffle square by~Theorem~\ref{thm:main-intro}. Hence the~subsequence is proper.

The~first block is $P_{16}$ from~Example~\ref{ex:first-decomposition}.  The~next block, written with~positions relative to~that block, is
\begin{align*}

The~support $I=\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,12\}$ and its complement both induce the~root $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{122121121}}$. The~third block is simply $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\boldsymbol{\mathsf{K}}}_{35}\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\boldsymbol{\mathsf{K}}}_{36}=\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{22}}$, with~root~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{2}}$. Hence the~first three cumulative endpoints are $16,34,36$.

Applying Listing~\ref{lst:residual-test} successively to~each shorter even-length candidate verifies that none works at~any displayed step.

label: lem:morph:odd-powers
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:morph:odd-powers}
Let $k_{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}}$ be a~positive odd integer for~each $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}\in A$. The~morphism $D:A^*\to A^*$ given by~$D(\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}})=\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}^{k_{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}}}$ reflects shuffle squares.

title: Proof

label: def:morph:private
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:morph:private}
A~symbol $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{b}}\in B$ is \emph{private to~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}$} for~a~morphism~$h$ if $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{b}}$ occurs in~$h(\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}})$ and does not occur in~$h(\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{c}})$ for~any $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{c}}\in A\setminus\{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}\}$.
head: environment

label: prop:morph:private-necessary
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:morph:private-necessary}
If a~nonerasing morphism $h:A^*\to B^*$ reflects shuffle squares, then every $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}\in A$ has a~private symbol. In~particular, $|B|\ge|A|$.

Suppose that for~each $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}\in A$ there is a~private symbol $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{b}}_{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}}$ whose multiplicity $k_{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}}=|h(\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}})|_{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{b}}_{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}}}$ is odd. Then $h$ reflects shuffle squares.

title: Proof
body_md: By~Proposition~\ref{prop:morph:private-necessary}, choose a~private symbol $\pi(\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}})$ for~each~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}$. These exhaust~$B$, so no symbol other than $\pi(\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}})$ can occur in~$h(\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}})$. Its multiplicity must be odd, since otherwise the~one-letter word~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}$ would have a~shuffle-square image. The~converse follows from~Lemma~\ref{lem:morph:odd-powers} and invariance under relabelling.

label: ex:morph:private
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:morph:private}
The~morphism given by~$h(\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}})=\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{2137}}$ and $h(\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{b}})=\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{4137}}$ reflects shuffle squares: the~private symbols $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{2}}$ and~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{4}}$ each have multiplicity~$1$, while the~symbols $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1}},\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{3}},\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{7}}$ occur in~both images. In~contrast, the~mere existence of~private symbols is not sufficient. The~morphism $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}\mapsto\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{11}}$, $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{b}}\mapsto\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{2}}$ has private symbols for~both letters but maps~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{a}}$ to~a~shuffle square. The~next criteria include cases in~which every symbol in~every image has even multiplicity.

label: lem:morph:path-cycle
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:morph:path-cycle}
Let an~ordered nest-free graph contain a~path~$P$ joining its first and last vertices. Every cycle vertex-disjoint from~$P$ has even length.
head: environment
name: Grytczuk--Pawlik--Ruci\'nski , Lemma 1

label: lem:morph:run-extraction
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:morph:run-extraction}
Let $H$ be a~word on~two distinct symbols~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{x}},\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{y}}$, containing~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{y}}$ and beginning and ending with~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{x}}$. Suppose that its first and last $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{x}}$-runs have odd lengths, every other $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{x}}$-run has even length, and all $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{y}}$-runs have the~same positive length~$q$. Given any nest-free perfect matching of~equal symbols on~the~positions of~$H$, one can select a~subset of~its edges that uses exactly one position from~each $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{y}}$-run and no $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{x}}$-positions.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Contract the~runs. The~resulting nest-free multigraph is the~disjoint union of~a~graph $G_{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{x}}}$ on~the~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{x}}$-runs and a~graph $G_{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{y}}}$ on~the~$\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{y}}$-runs, with~the~vertex order inherited from~$H$. Exactly the~first and last vertices of~$G_{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{x}}}$ have odd degree. They belong to~the~same connected component, since every component has an~even number of~odd-degree vertices. Hence $G_{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{x}}}$ contains a~path~$P$ joining the~extreme vertices of~the~whole graph.

The~graph $G_{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{y}}}$ has no loop: a~path from~the~first to~the~last vertex must have an~edge spanning the~vertex of~any such loop, which would create a~nest. By~Lemma~\ref{lem:morph:path-cycle}, $G_{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{y}}}$ also has no odd cycle of~length at~least three. Thus $G_{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{y}}}$ is bipartite. This is the~parity mechanism used in~the~proof of~\cite[Theorem~1]{GrytczukPawlikRucinskiPreprint}.

Every vertex of~$G_{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{y}}}$ has degree~$q$. If its bipartition is $L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R$, then counting edges gives $|L|=|R|$ and, for~each $S\subseteq L$,
\begin{align*}
 q|S|\le q|N(S)|.
\end{align*}
Hall's theorem therefore gives a~perfect matching of~$G_{\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{y}}}$. For~each edge of~this matching choose its corresponding edge in~the~original position matching. Exactly one position in~each $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{y}}$-run is selected, as~required.

label: rem:morph:attribution
title: Remark

\label{rem:morph:attribution}
For~a~single source letter, the~non-square assertion for~odd powers of~the~images in~Theorem~\ref{thm:morph:multirun} is already covered by~\cite[Corollary~3]{GrytczukPawlikRucinskiPreprint}. title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal R$ be the~set of~$230$ nonempty even-Parikh words in~Table~\ref{tab:C1-even-bad}. The~following finite checks suffice. For~each $r=\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{r}}_1\cdots \textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{r}}_n\in\mathcal R$, enumerate the~operations specified in~Table~\ref{repair:tab:finite-local}, and test the~result with Proposition~\ref{prop:residual-test}. In~the~last two rows, also require membership in~$\mathcal{C}^1$. Each row succeeds for~all~$230$ words. Listing~\ref{lst:repair-local} specifies these checks. They are performed independently by~\texttt{verify\_local\_repairs.py} after regenerating~$\mathcal R$.

By~Corollary~\ref{cor:C1-factorization}, write $w=S_1\cdots S_k r$, where $r\in\mathcal R$. Apply the~appropriate operation inside~$r$. The~resulting remainder is a~shuffle square, and concatenation with the~unchanged $S_i$ gives a~shuffle square. Distances from the~right endpoint are unchanged. In~(iii) and~(iv), the~finite checks leave the~first two letters of~$r$ unchanged. Thus they also preserve the~$C^1$ condition across the~boundary between $S_k$ and~$r$. All other boundaries are untouched.

For~sharpness, direct enumeration of~all eligible operations in~the~words of~Table~\ref{repair:tab:sharp-local} gives the~stated smallest window or suffix length. In~particular, the~successful transpositions for~the~first word start at~positions $1,3,8,10,15$. Among these, exactly $1,3,8,10$ preserve~$C^1$. The~successful pair deletions for~the~second word start at~positions $2,4,7,11,14$. These complete lists prove the~first three lower bounds. The~last lower bound follows by~checking both inserted pairs at~each of~the~last six gaps, and finding no repair in~$\mathcal{C}^1$ there. A~repair exists before the~suffix of~length~$6$. Reversal preserves shuffle squares and~$\mathcal{C}^1$ and converts all right-end assertions to~left-end assertions.

label: repair:rem:run-three
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{repair:rem:run-three}
The~single-repair conclusion does not extend unchanged to~words whose runs have length at~most~$3$. For~example, direct enumeration gives $\delta(\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{12221112}})=4$. Deleting an~equal pair from each of~its two length-$3$ runs leaves $\textcolor{purple!69!black}{\mathtt{1212}}$. Thus at~least two equal-pair deletions are needed in~this larger class. It is natural to~ask whether two such deletions suffice for~every even-Parikh word with run lengths at~most~$3$. The~results above do not settle this question.
